title: Sewage backing up into the basement when the power fails
summary: When the power fails, town sewage pumps stop and sewage rises out of the lowest drains first: basement floor drains, toilets and showers. Stop using water, plug or close the low drains, and if it gets in, treat it as live, germ-laden water and keep engines outside.

materials.item: Drain plugs sized to each basement drain: test balls, twist plugs or tapered rubber plugs
Inner tube, plywood or solid board, and 2×4s for bracing
materials.qty: for each drain without a plug

steps.text: When the power fails in town, cut water use at once: flush only for solids, no laundry or dishwashing, short showers at most, nothing poured down drains, and keep it up for about an hour after power returns (West Hants lift stations). Tell the households below you.
Find your lowest drains: basement floor drains, toilet, shower, tub, laundry tub and washer standpipe. Sewage comes out wherever a drain sits below the level in the sewer (NDSU AE1476).

If you have a backwater valve (in the floor near the main cleanout), make sure its gate moves freely and has no debris in it, since debris stops it sealing (NDSU AE1476, EPCOR backwater valve). Do that only while no sewage has come up yet, and put the cover back at once; if sewage is already rising, leave the cover on. If it's a manual knife or slice valve, close it (NDSU AE1476).
steps.warn: While the flap or valve is shut, no toilet, sink, shower, washer or dishwasher in the house can be used: your own wastewater comes up the floor drain (EPCOR backwater valve, NDSU AE1476).

steps.text: Plug each floor drain: lift the grate and fit a test ball, twist plug or tapered plug of the right size (NDSU AE1476).
steps.warn: Overtightening a plug can crack the pipe. A plug that pressure can push out needs bracing (NDSU AE1476). If water is already on the floor, don't wade in to fit one: switch the power off first, from a dry place.

steps.text: If a grate won't come off, lay a piece of inner tube over the drain, plywood on top, and wedge a 2×4 between it and a board against the ceiling (NDSU AE1476).
Plug or cap the other low fixtures: shower drains, tub and sink drains and overflows, the washer standpipe, and the basement toilet's pipe if you take the toilet off (NDSU AE1476).

On a septic system with a float-controlled pump chamber (a pressure-distribution system): cut water use to a minimum and, after 6 hours without power, switch the pump off at its panel. When power returns, run it 5 minutes at most every 6 hours until it stops by itself (WA DOH 337-087).
steps.warn: Never go into a pump chamber: its gases are poisonous and the lack of oxygen can be fatal (WA DOH 337-087). Tanks, manholes and lift stations are the same, and an estimated 60 % of confined-space deaths are would-be rescuers (CCOHS confined spaces).

steps.text: Switch the household to a bucket toilet until the sewer works again ([Toilets in winter](#guides/skill_toilets_in_winter)).

If sewage is already in the basement, stay out of the water and switch the power off from a dry place: the main breaker or disconnect, plus any generator, inverter or solar system feeding the house (York sewage backup, CDC flooded home). If you would have to step into the water to reach the panel, don't: CDC says to call an electrician and York says to ask the electrical utility (CDC flooded home, York sewage backup).
steps.warn: Never switch power or use an electric tool while standing in water (CDC flooded home). A generator, inverter or solar system can make the wiring live; a generator may feed house wiring only through approved transfer equipment (CDC flooded home, TSASK flood safety).

steps.text: If water reached a gas furnace, water heater, range or dryer, shut the gas off at the meter or propane tank and at each appliance valve, and don't relight anything that was under water (TSASK flood safety, Alberta gas and flooding). If you smell gas, open the windows, shut the main gas valve and leave, with no switches or flames (CDC flooded home). A flooded gas appliance can start a fire or make carbon monoxide, so with no gasfitter to check it, leave it off and heat the house another way ([Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm)).
Keep children, pets, anyone pregnant and anyone with breathing problems away from the sewage and everything it touched, until the clean-up is done (York sewage backup, CDC cleanup).
Put on rubber boots, rubber gloves, eye protection and a mask before you touch anything (York sewage backup, CDC cleanup).

Pump or bail it out; if the ground outside is soaked, take the water down in stages, about a third a day, or walls and floors can buckle (Red Cross flood guide). Run any engine pump, pressure washer or generator outside, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents (CDC flooded home).
steps.warn: Engines in a house, basement, garage, carport or porch kill with carbon monoxide, even with doors and windows open (CDC flooded home).

steps.text: Throw out soaked porous things (carpet, underlay, mattresses, upholstered furniture, books, soft toys) and soaked drywall and insulation (York sewage backup, CDC cleanup). Wash hard surfaces with soap and water, then wet them with plain unscented 5.25 % bleach, 100 mL in 1 L of water (bleach into the water), and keep them wet for at least 10 minutes (York sewage backup, CDC cleanup). For 6 % or 8.25 % bleach use the amounts in [Sanitation and hygiene](#ref/reference_sanitation/bleach_solutions).
steps.warn: Never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or other acids, or any other cleaner, such as glass or toilet-bowl cleaner: the gas is toxic (Health Canada bleach, York sewage backup). Open windows and doors first (CDC cleanup).

steps.text: Dry the space with open windows and fans, within 24 to 48 hours if you can (CDC cleanup, York sewage backup). From a dry place, switch off the breakers for any wiring the water reached before the power comes back, and don't use a wet socket, appliance or panel until it is completely dry and checked; a panel that was under water has to be replaced or fully cleaned (CDC flooded home, TSASK flood safety, Red Cross flood guide).

Wash with soap and clean water after every session, throw out any food the sewage touched, and watch for diarrhoea, vomiting or fever (York sewage backup). Wash the clothes you wore in hot water and detergent, apart from clean laundry (CDC cleanup). If sewage got into a cut or sore, wash it well with soap and clean water (York sewage backup, CDC wound care); a cut that faeces or soil got into counts as tetanus-prone, so a booster is due if your last shot was 5 or more years ago (Canadian Immunization Guide). Redness, swelling, oozing, fever or growing pain means infection (CDC wound care).

notes:
## Why it happens when the power goes

Many towns move sewage through pumping (lift) stations, and those pumps need power all the time. When the power fails, the small reserve in each station fills quickly, and sewage can back up into streets, basements and waterways. Most ordinary stations may have only a high-level alarm, not backup power (West Hants lift stations). Heavy rain or flooding does the same where storm water and sewage share pipes, or where the treatment plant is flooded (NDSU AE1476).

## Who gets it first

Sewage finds the lowest opening. Once it stands higher in the sewer than a drain in your house, it comes out of that drain (NDSU AE1476). That is usually a basement floor drain (EPCOR backwater valve), but basement toilets, showers, tubs, sinks, laundry tubs and washing-machine drains are all ways in (NDSU AE1476). So the lowest houses on the street, and basement suites, get it first, and the water flushed upstairs in your own house and the houses uphill is part of what is rising.

West Hants asks people to cut water use the moment the power goes: no laundry or dishwasher, short showers, flush only for solids, pour nothing down drains, and keep it up for about an hour after the power comes back while the stations pump down (West Hants lift stations).

## Backwater valves

A backwater valve sits on the main sewer pipe from the house and has a flap that closes by itself when sewage flows back from the street. EPCOR says backwater valves weren't required in homes built before 1989, so an older house may not have one (EPCOR backwater valve). Look in the basement floor near the main cleanout (NDSU AE1476).
- **While the flap is shut, nothing can leave the house either.** Don't use any toilet, sink, shower, washer or dishwasher: your own wastewater has nowhere to go but up the floor drain (EPCOR backwater valve).
- Some houses have a manual slice or knife valve instead, reached through a hatch in the basement floor. Closed, it stops flow both ways, so no water can be used in the house at all (NDSU AE1476).
- Debris in the gate stops it sealing: check and clean it (EPCOR backwater valve) at least once a year (NDSU AE1476). Do it well before an outage; if sewage is already rising, leave the cover on.

## Plugs

| Plug | How it works | Water can still drain? |
|---|---|---|
| Test ball | Pushed into the pipe and pumped up with air to its rated pressure | No (NDSU AE1476) |
| Twist plug | Pushed in, then a wing nut is turned until it's tight; plastic or metal; floor, shower and toilet drains | No (NDSU AE1476) |
| Pressure plug | Tapered rubber or wooden plug forced in; may need bracing | No (NDSU AE1476) |
| Float backflow plug | A ball or float seals the pipe when sewage rises; can stay in all year | Yes (NDSU AE1476) |
| Threaded cap | Screwed onto the pipe after the fixture comes off | No (NDSU AE1476) |

The float type suits a floor drain that also takes a high-efficiency furnace's condensate (NDSU AE1476). Measure the pipe before you need a plug: sizes vary (NDSU AE1476). No plug at all? A flexible rubber ball just bigger than the pipe, braced in place, works in an emergency (NDSU AE1476).

## Septic systems

Some rural septic systems pump the effluent from a chamber out to the field. When that pump stops, the chamber's reserve fills; once it's full, the plumbing in the house backs up. If the pump is float-controlled and off more than 6 hours (timer controls correct this on their own), cut water use to a minimum and switch the pump off at its control panel; when power returns, run it 5 minutes at most, then off, every 6 hours until it shuts off by itself (WA DOH 337-087). Never go into the pump chamber: its gases are poisonous and the lack of oxygen can kill (WA DOH 337-087). The same goes for a septic tank, manhole or a town lift station's wet well: see [Confined spaces](#browse/hazards/confined_space) and [Hydrogen sulphide](#browse/hazards/h2s).

## Sewage in the basement: what can hurt you

- **Germs.** Sewage carries bacteria, protozoa and other germs (NDSU AE1476). Children, pregnant women and people with breathing problems shouldn't handle it or anything it touched (York sewage backup). Keep children and pets out of the affected area until the clean-up is finished (CDC cleanup). See [Medical waste and sewage](#browse/hazards/biohazard).
- **Live water.** Stay out of sewage water near outlets and wiring, and turn the power off at the breaker if water stands or wires may get wet (York sewage backup). Switch it off from a dry place; if you would have to step into the water to reach the main switch, don't (CDC flooded home). Never switch power on or off, or use an electric tool, while standing in water (CDC flooded home). Wiring, sockets and appliances that got wet must be completely dry and checked before use, and a service panel that was under water has to be replaced or fully cleaned (CDC flooded home, TSASK flood safety). With the grid down, a generator, inverter or solar system can still make the wiring live ([mains](#browse/hazards/mains), [Make a circuit dead](#guides/safety_mains_isolation)).
- **Carbon monoxide.** Gas-engine pumps, pressure washers and generators never run inside a house, basement, garage, carport or porch, or within 6 m (20 ft) of a door, window or vent, even with them open (CDC flooded home). See [Carbon monoxide](#browse/hazards/co_gas).
- **Gas appliances.** A furnace, water heater or other gas appliance that was under water can cause fire, explosion and carbon monoxide hazards. Shut the gas off at the meter or propane tank and at the appliance valves, never relight anything that was under water, and leave it off until a gas contractor has checked it (TSASK flood safety, Alberta gas and flooding). With none to be had, leave it off and heat the house another way ([Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm)). If you smell gas, open the windows, shut the main gas valve and leave, with no switches or flames (CDC flooded home).
- **Mould.** Assume a house that was flooded and closed up for several days has mould (CDC flooded home). Open doors and windows and let it air for at least 30 minutes before you stay, and dry it out fast, with fans blowing out of a window rather than into the house (CDC flooded home). For mould clean-up wear an N95 or better and goggles (CDC cleanup). See [Mould](#browse/hazards/mold).
- **Food and wells.** Throw out food that sewage touched, including canned, bottled, fridge and freezer food. Don't use a private well that sewage may have reached for drinking, cooking or bathing until it has been tested (York sewage backup); with no lab, see [Shock-chlorinate a well](#guides/skill_shock_chlorinate_well).

## Cleaning up

Wear rubber boots, rubber gloves, eye protection and a mask (York sewage backup, CDC cleanup). Assume everything sewage touched is contaminated: clean and disinfect it, or throw it out (York sewage backup).
- **Throw out:** mattresses, carpet and underlay, rugs, upholstered furniture, pillows, stuffed and baby toys, soothers and bottle nipples, wooden cutting boards, foam-rubber items, books, wall coverings and cosmetics (York sewage backup), and drywall and insulation the sewage soaked (CDC cleanup).
- **Clean, then disinfect:** hard floors, concrete, sealed wood and drywall, trim, metal and plastic furniture, appliances, sinks and toys: wash with soap and clean water first, then bleach, and rinse toys well with clean water afterwards (York sewage backup).
- **Bleach mix:** 100 mL of 5.25 % household bleach in 1 L of water (5,000 ppm), always bleach into water, left wet at least 10 minutes, made fresh daily, with fans or open windows. Never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or other acids, or any other cleaner, including glass and toilet-bowl cleaners: the gas is toxic (Health Canada bleach, York sewage backup). Other strengths are in [Sanitation and hygiene](#ref/reference_sanitation/bleach_solutions).
- **Dry it:** open doors and windows and run fans (York sewage backup), within 24 to 48 hours if you can (CDC cleanup).
- **You:** wash with soap and clean water after every session, and clean any cut that sewage touched with soap and clean water (York sewage backup, CDC wound care). If there is no soap and clean water, use an alcohol hand sanitiser of 70 to 90 % (York sewage backup). Wash the clothes you wore in hot water with detergent, apart from clean laundry (CDC cleanup). A cut that faeces or soil got into is a tetanus-prone wound: a booster is due if your last tetanus shot was 5 or more years ago (10 for a clean, minor wound), and anyone who never had a full set needs a clinic for the shot and immune globulin (Canadian Immunization Guide). Redness, swelling, oozing, fever or growing pain means infection and needs medical care (CDC wound care). Diarrhoea, vomiting or fever after contact with sewage needs a doctor if one can be reached (York sewage backup).

## When no help is coming

There is no public works crew, plumber or health inspector, so prevention is the whole job.
- **Before it happens:** buy or make plugs for every basement drain now, and practise fitting them (NDSU AE1476). Find your backwater valve or knife valve and clean it.
- **The day the power fails:** stop flushing and draining, upstairs as well as down; tell the households below you. Move to a bucket toilet ([Toilets in winter](#guides/skill_toilets_in_winter), [Sanitation and hygiene](#ref/reference_sanitation/bucket_toilet)).
- **No plug fits:** a piece of inner tube over the drain, plywood or solid board on top (not particle board, which crumbles when wet), and a 2×4 wedged up to a board against the ceiling holds the seal down (NDSU AE1476).
- **A basement toilet you don't need:** take it off and plug or cap the pipe, and do it before sewage comes up (NDSU AE1476 says to prepare well in advance); if sewage is already in the bowl, leave the toilet where it is. NDSU's steps: water off, supply line off, flush the tank empty, empty the bowl, unbolt it (cut any caulk with a utility knife), scrape off the old wax ring, and plug the pipe. It goes back on later with a new wax ring (NDSU AE1476).
- **Sewage already in:** cut every source of power from a dry spot first; if the panel stands in water, don't go to it, and stay out of the water too until the power is known to be off (CDC flooded home). Bail with lidded buckets and carry it to a pit or trench at the distances in [Sanitation and hygiene](#ref/reference_sanitation/latrines_and_distances). Any engine pump goes outside, 6 m (20 ft) from openings (CDC flooded home); run only the hose into the house.
- **Winter:** standing sewage in a basement that's below freezing can turn to ice and be harder to clear, so deal with it while you can still work in there, and watch for ice on the floor and stairs.
- **After:** watch everyone who cleaned up for diarrhoea, vomiting or fever; see [Dehydration and diarrhoea](#ref/reference_first_aid/dehydration_and_diarrhoea).
